claim: Misfolded prion protein (PrP*) is used as a model to investigate how mammalian cells recognize and degrade misfolded GPI-anchored proteins.
source: We have used misfolded prion protein (PrP*) as a model to investigate how mammalian cells recognize and degrade misfolded GPI-anchored proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the experimental approach of the study.

claim: Most misfolded membrane proteins are degraded by proteasomes.
source: While most misfolded membrane proteins are degraded by proteasomes, misfolded GPI-anchored proteins are primarily degraded in lysosomes.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge to contrast with the findings about GPI-anchored proteins.

claim: Misfolded GPI-anchored proteins are primarily degraded in lysosomes.
source: While most misfolded membrane proteins are degraded by proteasomes, misfolded GPI-anchored proteins are primarily degraded in lysosomes.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: At least 85% of PrP* molecules transiently access the plasma membrane en route to lysosomes.
source: Quantitative flow cytometry analysis showed that at least 85% of PrP* molecules transiently access the plasma membrane en route to lysosomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from flow cytometry experiments described in the abstract.

claim: PrP* has a remarkably invariant interactome during its trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to lysosomes.
source: Unexpectedly, time-resolved quantitative proteomics revealed a remarkably invariant PrP* interactome during its trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to lysosomes.
evidence: This is a key finding from quantitative proteomics experiments described in the abstract.

claim: PrP* arrives at the plasma membrane in complex with ER-derived chaperones and cargo receptors.
source: Hence, PrP* arrives at the plasma membrane in complex with ER-derived chaperones and cargo receptors.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by proteomic and biochemical data.

claim: ER-derived interaction partners are critical for rapid endocytosis of PrP*.
source: These interaction partners were critical for rapid endocytosis because a GPI-anchored protein induced to misfold at the cell surface was not recognized effectively for degradation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with FKBP* that was induced to misfold at the cell surface.

claim: A GPI-anchored protein induced to misfold at the cell surface is not recognized effectively for degradation.
source: These interaction partners were critical for rapid endocytosis because a GPI-anchored protein induced to misfold at the cell surface was not recognized effectively for degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FKBP*-YFP-GPI Shield1 withdrawal experiments.

claim: Resident ER factors have post-ER itineraries that shield misfolded GPI-anchored proteins during their trafficking.
source: Thus, resident ER factors have post-ER itineraries that not only shield misfolded GPI-anchored proteins during their trafficking, but also provide a quality control cue at the cell surface for endocytic routing to lysosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the invariant interactome data and surface detection of ER chaperones.

claim: Resident ER factors provide a quality control cue at the cell surface for endocytic routing to lysosomes.
source: Thus, resident ER factors have post-ER itineraries that not only shield misfolded GPI-anchored proteins during their trafficking, but also provide a quality control cue at the cell surface for endocytic routing to lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteins misfolded at the surface without ER factors are not efficiently degraded.

claim: Over 150 proteins in the human genome are anchored to the cell surface solely by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor in the membrane.
source: Over 150 proteins in the human genome are anchored to the cell surface solely by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor in the membrane (UniProt Consortium, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from the UniProt Consortium database.

claim: GPI-anchored proteins are ubiquitous across eukaryotes, often highly abundant, and have diverse roles including cell adhesion, signaling, intercellular communication, and enzymatic reactions.
source: GPI-anchored proteins are ubiquitous across eukaryotes, often highly abundant, and have diverse roles including cell adhesion, signaling, intercellular communication, and enzymatic reactions (Kinoshita et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Kinoshita et al., 2008.

claim: Mammalian prion protein (PrP) can cause neurodegenerative disease when misfolded variants accumulate in cells.
source: The importance of this problem is highlighted by the capacity of mammalian prion protein (PrP), a widely expressed and conserved GPI-anchored protein, to cause neurodegenerative disease when misfolded variants accumulate in cells (Prusiner, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Prusiner, 2013.

claim: Errors in targeting GPI-anchored proteins to the ER are handled by cytosolic degradation pathways.
source: Errors in targeting GPI-anchored proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or processing their signal for GPI anchor attachment at the membrane are handled by cytosolic (Ast et al., 2014; Hessa et al., 2011) and ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathways (Ali et al., 2000; Ashok and Hegde, 2008; Sikorska et al., 2016; Wilbourn et al., 1998), respectively.
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Ast et al., 2014; Hessa et al., 2011).

claim: Errors in processing GPI anchor attachment signals are handled by ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathways.
source: Errors in targeting GPI-anchored proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or processing their signal for GPI anchor attachment at the membrane are handled by cytosolic (Ast et al., 2014; Hessa et al., 2011) and ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathways (Ali et al., 2000; Ashok and Hegde, 2008; Sikorska et al., 2016; Wilbourn et al., 1998), respectively.
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Ali et al., 2000; Ashok and Hegde, 2008; Sikorska et al., 2016; Wilbourn et al., 1998).

claim: In yeast, once the GPI anchor is added, the misfolded protein is not degraded via Hrd1p.
source: Early studies in yeast suggested that once the GPI anchor is added, the misfolded protein is not degraded via Hrd1p (Fujita et al., 2006), a central ERAD factor that mediates ubiquitination and retrotranslocation of substrates from the ER to the cytosol (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016; Bays et al., 2001; Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Fujita et al., 2006.

claim: Hrd1p is a central ERAD factor that mediates ubiquitination and retrotranslocation of substrates from the ER to the cytosol.
source: Early studies in yeast suggested that once the GPI anchor is added, the misfolded protein is not degraded via Hrd1p (Fujita et al., 2006), a central ERAD factor that mediates ubiquitination and retrotranslocation of substrates from the ER to the cytosol (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016; Bays et al., 2001; Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016; Bays et al., 2001; Stein et al., 2014).

claim: Misfolded GPI-anchored proteins in yeast use a pathway dependent on ER-to-Golgi transport.
source: Instead, misfolded GPI-anchored proteins in yeast were suggested to use a seemingly unconventional pathway dependent on ER-to-Golgi transport (Fujita et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Fujita et al., 2006.

claim: ER export receptors of the TMED family rapidly sequester GPI-anchored proteins to prevent their engagement by Hrd1p, thereby allowing degradation in the vacuole.
source: Subsequent analysis suggested that ER export receptors of the TMED family (also known as the p24 family) rapidly sequester GPI-anchored proteins to prevent their engagement by Hrd1p, thereby allowing degradation in the vacuole (Sikorska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Sikorska et al., 2016.

claim: The GPI-anchored protein is primarily degraded by ERAD when the TMED cargo receptor is eliminated.
source: The GPI-anchored protein was primarily degraded by ERAD when the TMED cargo receptor was eliminated.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from yeast studies, implying citation support from the preceding context.

claim: The primary pathway for GPI-anchored protein degradation in yeast is via trafficking to the vacuole, with ERAD serving as a failsafe pathway when the vacuole route is impaired.
source: Thus, the primary pathway for GPI-anchored protein degradation in yeast is via trafficking to the vacuole, with ERAD serving as a failsafe pathway when the vacuole route is impaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited yeast studies.

claim: Human disease-causing PrP mutants are not degraded by ERAD, do not depend on the proteasome, and exit the ER despite their misfolding.
source: First, investigation of the localization, trafficking, and turnover of a panel of human disease-causing PrP mutants showed that they are not degraded by ERAD, do not depend on the proteasome, and exit the ER despite their misfolding (Ashok and Hegde, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Ashok and Hegde, 2009.

claim: The misfolded population of mutant PrP is selectively observed in post-ER intracellular compartments en route to their ultimate degradation in acidic compartments presumed to be lysosomes.
source: The misfolded population of mutant PrP was selectively observed in post-ER intracellular compartments en route to their ultimate degradation in acidic compartments presumed to be lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies on mutant PrP.

claim: PrP* is primarily retained in the ER at steady state but can be released into the secretory pathway by acute ER stress.
source: This study showed that PrP* is primarily retained in the ER at steady state but can be released into the secretory pathway by acute ER stress.
evidence: This is cited from Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014.

claim: Transit of PrP* to the Golgi requires cargo receptor TMED10.
source: Transit of PrP* to the Golgi requires cargo receptor TMED10 (also known as Tmp21, or p24δ1) with which it interacts in co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014.

claim: At least a subpopulation of PrP* transits the cell surface based on extracellular antibody uptake assays and trapping of PrP* at the cell surface after cholesterol depletion.
source: At least a subpopulation was implicated in transiting the cell surface based on extracellular antibody uptake assays and trapping of PrP* at the cell surface after cholesterol depletion (Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014.

claim: Exposing misfolded proteins to the extracellular environment can be detrimental.
source: The proportion of PrP* using this itinerary was unclear but it is important to understand because exposing misfolded proteins to the extracellular environment can be detrimental.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about protein quality control.

claim: Surface-exposed misfolded forms of PrP may facilitate uptake of prions into cells.
source: In the specific case of PrP, surface-exposed misfolded forms may facilitate uptake of prions into cells (Fehlinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Fehlinger et al., 2017.

claim: Both folded and misfolded GPI-anchored proteins engage TMED family export receptors at the ER and traffic to the Golgi.
source: From these combined studies in yeast and mammalian cells, it is thought that both folded and misfolded GPI-anchored proteins engage TMED family export receptors at the ER and traffic to the Golgi.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the cited studies.

claim: At some step at or after the trans-Golgi network, the itineraries of folded and misfolded GPI-anchored proteins diverge.
source: At some step at or after the trans-Golgi network, their itineraries diverge.
evidence: This is inferred from the different fates of folded vs. misfolded GPI-anchored proteins.

claim: Folded GPI-anchored proteins go on to reside at the cell surface.
source: Folded GPI-anchored proteins go on to reside at the cell surface, whereas misfolded variants are delivered to the lysosome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GPI-anchored protein trafficking.

claim: Misfolded GPI-anchored proteins are delivered to the lysosome.
source: Folded GPI-anchored proteins go on to reside at the cell surface, whereas misfolded variants are delivered to the lysosome.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by the data in this study.

claim: The steady state level of GFP-PrP* is very similar to GFP-PrP.
source: Immunoblotting of total cell lysates after induction with doxycycline showed that the steady state level of GFP-PrP* was very similar to GFP-PrP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting data in Figure 1A.

claim: GFP-PrP has complex glycosylation due to its transit through the Golgi.
source: The different migration patterns are due to complex glycosylation of GFP-PrP during its transit through the Golgi in contrast to core-glycosylated GFP-PrP* primarily retained in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the migration patterns on the gel and knowledge of glycosylation in different compartments.

claim: GFP-PrP* has core glycosylation and is primarily retained in the ER.
source: The different migration patterns are due to complex glycosylation of GFP-PrP during its transit through the Golgi in contrast to core-glycosylated GFP-PrP* primarily retained in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the migration patterns on the gel and knowledge of glycosylation in different compartments.

claim: Total GFP-PrP* is almost identical to GFP-PrP as measured by flow cytometry.
source: Consistent with the immunoblotting, flow cytometry of GFP fluorescence showed that total GFP-PrP* was almost identical to GFP-PrP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 1B.

claim: GFP-PrP* is primarily localized intracellularly in a pattern consistent with the ER.
source: As expected from earlier studies (Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014), GFP-PrP* was primarily localized intracellularly in a pattern consistent with the ER, while GFP-PrP was primarily at the cell surface (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 1C and is consistent with cited earlier studies.

claim: GFP-PrP is primarily localized at the cell surface.
source: As expected from earlier studies (Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014), GFP-PrP* was primarily localized intracellularly in a pattern consistent with the ER, while GFP-PrP was primarily at the cell surface (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon induction of acute ER stress with thapsigargin, ~80% of GFP-PrP* is degraded after three hours.
source: Upon induction of acute ER stress with thapsigargin (Tg),~80% of GFP-PrP* was degraded after three hours (Figure 1D, upper panel).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D.

claim: GFP-PrP* degradation is almost completely inhibited by Bafilomycin A1.
source: This degradation was almost completely inhibited by Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1), which prevents lysosome acidification and reduces proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1D and demonstrates lysosomal degradation.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 prevents lysosome acidification and reduces proteolytic activity.
source: This degradation was almost completely inhibited by Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1), which prevents lysosome acidification and reduces proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is stated as the known mechanism of action of Bafilomycin A1.

claim: GFP-PrP is not affected by thapsigargin and is only slightly stabilized by BafA1.
source: By contrast, GFP-PrP was not affected by Tg and was only slightly stabilized by BafA1 (Figure 1D, lower panel) consistent with its slow turnover from the cell surface in lysosomes.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D.

claim: GFP-PrP has slow turnover from the cell surface in lysosomes.
source: By contrast, GFP-PrP was not affected by Tg and was only slightly stabilized by BafA1 (Figure 1D, lower panel) consistent with its slow turnover from the cell surface in lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the BafA1 stabilization data.

claim: GFP-PrP* traffics via the Golgi to lysosomes after ER stress.
source: Based on earlier work (Satpute-Krishnan et al., 2014), this corresponds to GFP-PrP* trafficking via the Golgi to lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from microscopy showing re-localization from ER to peri-nuclear structure to cytosolic puncta (Figure 1E) and cited earlier work.

claim: Brefeldin A causes ER retention of GFP-PrP* and precludes trafficking to lysosomes.
source: While Brefeldin A (BFA) causes ER retention of GFP-PrP* and precludes trafficking to lysosomes (as verified by microscopy; data not shown), degradation still proceeds, albeit somewhat less efficiently (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of ER export, GFP-PrP* is eventually degraded by ERAD.
source: Based on earlier studies in yeast (Sikorska et al., 2016), it is likely that in the absence of ER export, GFP-PrP* is eventually degraded by ERAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the BFA data and cited yeast studies.

claim: Cells expressing GFP-PrP* contain a surface population whose level is between one-twentieth and one-fiftieth of cells expressing GFP-PrP.
source: Using saturating concentrations of extracellular Nb, we found that cells expressing GFP-PrP* contain a clearly detectable surface population whose level is between one-twentieth and one-fiftieth of cells expressing GFP-PrP (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells expressing GFP-PrP* yield one-twentieth the amount of Nb relative to cells expressing GFP-PrP.
source: Cells expressing GFP-PrP* yielded one-twentieth the amount of Nb relative to cells expressing GFP-PrP (50 pg and 1 ng, respectively).
evidence: This is quantified from the Nb purification experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Surface-bound Nb does not exchange antigens after cell lysis.
source: Importantly, control experiments in which lysate from Nb-labeled cells was mixed with lysates containing free GFP showed that free GFP was not recovered in the Nb-purified complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). This verified that surface-bound Nb does not exchange antigens after cell lysis over the time frame needed for affinity purification of Nb-antigen complexes.
evidence: This is shown by the control experiment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 20-fold more PrP resides at the cell surface than PrP*.
source: Thus, 20-fold more PrP resides at the cell surface than PrP*.
evidence: This is calculated from the quantitative Nb binding data.

claim: 87% of total GFP-PrP is at the cell surface.
source: Based on sensitivity to extracellular trypsin, we could determine that 87% of total GFP-PrP is at the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is determined from the trypsin digestion experiment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The surface level of GFP-PrP* increases when endocytosis is impaired by knocking down AP2.
source: First, the surface level increased when endocytosis was impaired by either knocking down AP2 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) or expressing a dominant-negative Dynamin (Damke et al., 2001) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 2E.

claim: The surface level of GFP-PrP* increases when endocytosis is impaired by expressing a dominant-negative Dynamin.
source: First, the surface level increased when endocytosis was impaired by either knocking down AP2 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) or expressing a dominant-negative Dynamin (Damke et al., 2001) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F and cited from Damke et al., 2001.

claim: The surface population of GFP-PrP* is decreased to near-background levels by blocking ER exit with BFA for two hours.
source: Second, the surface population was decreased to near-background levels by blocking ER exit with BFA for two hours (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 2G.

claim: Almost all of the surface population of GFP-PrP* contains immature glycans.
source: Curiously, almost all of the surface population of GFP-PrP* contains immature glycans (Figure 2D) despite having trafficked through the Golgi (see Discussion).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2D.

claim: The nanobody taken into GFP-PrP* cells slightly exceeds the GFP-PrP fluorescence standard.
source: We observed that the nanobody taken into GFP-PrP* cells (Figure 3B, red trace) slightly exceeded the GFP-PrP fluorescence standard (Figure 3B, blue trace).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: For GFP-PrP* cells to accumulate an amount of nanobody comparable to the fluorescence standard, ~86% of the intracellular population would need to access and trap extracellular nanobody.
source: Thus, for GFP-PrP* cells to accumulate an amount of nanobody comparable to the fluorescence standard,~86% of the intracellular population would need to access and trap extracellular nanobody.
evidence: This is calculated from the Nb uptake data and the known surface levels.

claim: The vast majority of initially intracellular GFP-PrP* must access the cell surface on its way to lysosomes during stress-triggered degradation.
source: Given that Nb accumulation in GFP-PrP* cells actually exceeds the GFP-PrP standard (Figure 3B), we conclude that the vast majority of initially intracellular GFP-PrP* must access the cell surface on its way to lysosomes during stress-triggered degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the Nb uptake exceeding the calculated threshold.

claim: Nb uptake by GFP-PrP* displays a lag of ~30 min consistent with the transit time for GFP-PrP* from the ER to the cell surface.
source: As expected for a trafficking itinerary via the Golgi, Nb uptake displayed a lag of ~30 min consistent with the transit time for GFP-PrP* from the ER to the cell surface (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the time course data in Figure 3C.

claim: GFP-PrP* accesses the cell surface at steady state similarly to what is observed during stress.
source: In the absence of ER stress, GFP-PrP* cells also take up extracellular nanobody selectively when GFP-PrP* is expressed (Figure 3C). This suggests that even at steady state, GFP-PrP* accesses the cell surface similarly to what is observed during stress.
evidence: This is shown by the Nb uptake data in Figure 3C.

claim: The rate of surface access is ~6 fold higher during acute ER stress than at steady state.
source: The slopes of the uptake time courses between 30 and 90 min suggest that the rate of surface access is ~6 fold higher during acute ER stress than at steady state.
evidence: This is calculated from the slopes of the uptake curves in Figure 3C.

claim: TMED10 is required for GFP-PrP* export from the ER under stressed conditions.
source: Fluorescence microscopy showed that in ∆TMED10 cells, acute ER stress no longer caused GFP-PrP* egress from the ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and sharply impaired uptake of extracellular Nb (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy and Nb uptake data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and Figure 3D.

claim: TMED10 is required for GFP-PrP* export from the ER under unstressed conditions.
source: Using the uptake assay, we found that Nb accumulation was also impaired under non-stressed conditions, further suggesting that the same pathway is used, albeit at a lower rate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by Nb uptake data in Figure 3E.

claim: TMED10 deletion has little or no effect on the amount of GFP-PrP trafficked to the cell surface.
source: Importantly, little or no effect was observed on the amount of GFP-PrP trafficked to the cell surface in ∆TMED10 cells (Figure 3F) indicating that neither trafficking nor GPI-anchored protein biogenesis are appreciably impaired.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3F.

claim: Both PrP* and PrP interact with TMED10 by coimmunoprecipitation.
source: Thus, although both PrP* and PrP interact with TMED10 by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), only PrP* strongly relies on it for lysosomal degradation via the cell surface.
evidence: This is shown by coimmunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Only PrP* strongly relies on TMED10 for lysosomal degradation via the cell surface.
source: Thus, although both PrP* and PrP interact with TMED10 by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), only PrP* strongly relies on it for lysosomal degradation via the cell surface.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of TMED10 deletion on PrP* vs. PrP trafficking.

claim: TMED10 sedimentation through a sucrose gradient suggests a native size larger than its 24 kD molecular weight.
source: TMED10 sedimentation through a sucrose gradient suggests a native size larger than its 24 kD molecular weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), consistent with it being part of a multi-protein complex (Jenne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: TMED10 is part of a multi-protein complex.
source: TMED10 sedimentation through a sucrose gradient suggests a native size larger than its 24 kD molecular weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), consistent with it being part of a multi-protein complex (Jenne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is inferred from the sucrose gradient data and cited from Jenne et al., 2002.

claim: The coiled-coil region of the TMED family is important for homo- and hetero-typic interactions.
source: Earlier work suggested that the coiled-coil region of the TMED family is important for homo- and hetero-typic interactions (Ciufo and Boyd, 2000; Emery et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Ciufo and Boyd, 2000 and Emery et al., 2000.

claim: TMED10 lacking the coiled-coil domain is completely inactive in rescuing GFP-PrP* trafficking.
source: While ∆TMED10 cells rescued with wild type TMED10 largely recovered Nb uptake by GFP-PrP* (Figure 3D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), ∆CC was completely inactive (Figure 4A) despite unimpaired interaction with GFP-PrP* (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by the Nb uptake data in Figure 4A.

claim: TMED10 lacking the coiled-coil domain has unimpaired interaction with GFP-PrP*.
source: While ∆TMED10 cells rescued with wild type TMED10 largely recovered Nb uptake by GFP-PrP* (Figure 3D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), ∆CC was completely inactive (Figure 4A) despite unimpaired interaction with GFP-PrP* (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by coimmunoprecipitation data in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of the lumenal GOLD domain is functional in restoring GFP-PrP* trafficking to ∆TMED10 cells.
source: Of note, deletion of the lumenal GOLD domain implicated in protein-protein interactions of uncertain relevance was functional in restoring GFP-PrP* trafficking to ∆TMED10 cells (data not shown) and unimpaired in its interaction with GFP-PrP* (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by the interaction data in Figure 4B and stated functional rescue.

claim: GFP-PrP* trafficking relies on a complex of multiple homologous TMED family proteins.
source: These observations can be explained if GFP-PrP* trafficking relies on a complex of multiple homologous TMED family proteins, more than one of which can interact with GFP-PrP*.
evidence: This is inferred from the coiled-coil deletion data showing loss of function despite retained PrP* binding.

claim: ∆TMED10 cells have reduced levels of TMED2.
source: Consistent with TMED10 interacting with other TMED family member(s), ∆TMED10 cells had reduced levels of TMED2, a putative part of the complex (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 4C.

claim: Reduced TMED2 in ∆TMED10 cells is partially restored upon acute re-introduction of TMED10 by transient transfection.
source: Reduced TMED2 is partially restored upon acute re-introduction of TMED10 by transient transfection, but not by re-introduction of the ∆CC mutant defective in hetero-typic TMED family interactions.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4C.

claim: The phenotype of ∆TMED10 cells cannot be rescued by TMED2 over-expression.
source: Notably, the phenotype of ∆TMED10 cells cannot be rescued by TMED2 over-expression arguing against TMED2 loss as the sole basis of impaired GFP-PrP* trafficking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In addition to TMED10, TMED2 is strongly required for GFP-PrP* trafficking.
source: Analysis of Nb uptake by GFP-PrP* in cells treated with siRNAs against each TMED family member suggests that in addition to TMED10, TMED2 is strongly required (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is shown by siRNA knockdown data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: A weaker phenotype is observed with at least one siRNA for both TMED5 and TMED9, but not TMED7.
source: A weaker phenotype is observed with at least one siRNA for both TMED5 and TMED9, but not TMED7.
evidence: This is shown by the siRNA knockdown data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The combination of TMED2/5/9/10 was previously reported to participate in the ER exit of GPI-anchored proteins.
source: The combination of TMED2/5/9/10 was previously reported to participate in the ER exit of GPI-anchored proteins (Fujita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Fujita et al., 2011.

claim: GFP-PrP* trafficking requires TMED2 and TMED10, possibly in a complex that also includes TMED5 and TMED9.
source: Our findings suggest that GFP-PrP* trafficking similarly requires TMED2 and TMED10, possibly in a complex that also includes TMED5 and TMED9.
evidence: This is concluded from the siRNA knockdown data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: GFP-PrP* specifically co-precipitates a variety of proteins that are reduced or absent from cells expressing GFP-PrP.
source: As observed in two examples (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), GFP-PrP* specifically co-precipitated a variety of proteins that were reduced or absent from cells expressing GFP-PrP.
evidence: This is shown by the stained gels in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified a number of ER-resident chaperones that were co-precipitated preferentially with GFP-PrP*.
source: As expected for a misfolding mutant, mass spectrometry identified a number of ER-resident chaperones that were co-precipitated preferentially with GFP-PrP*.
evidence: This is stated as a result from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The most abundant chaperones co-precipitated with GFP-PrP* are Calnexin (CNX) and BiP.
source: The most abundant of these were Calnexin (CNX) and BiP (also called GRP78), with lesser amounts of GRP94 (also called endoplasmin), protein disulphide isomerase (PDI), ERP57 (an oxidoredutase that cooperates with CNX), and ERP72.
evidence: This is stated as a result from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Ten proteins showed a WT/KO ratio of at least 1.4 from all three TMT experiments comparing wild type and ∆TMED10 cells.
source: Ten proteins showed a WT/KO ratio of least 1.4 (i.e., Log2 of 0.5) from all three TMT experiments, and another 11 proteins exceeded this threshold in two of three experiments (six were found in the experiment displayed in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from quantitative mass spectrometry shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Of the 21 proteins with elevated WT/KO ratios, seven were TMED family members involved in bidirectional trafficking between the ER and Golgi.
source: Of these 21 proteins, seven were TMED family members involved in bidirectional trafficking between the ER and Golgi.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the quantitative mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The four family members implicated in functional assays of GFP-PrP* trafficking (TMED10, TMED2, TMED5, and TMED9) were among the proteins enriched in wild type cells in all three TMT experiments.
source: Notably, the four family members implicated in functional assays of GFP-PrP* trafficking (TMED10, TMED2, TMED5, and TMED9) were among the proteins enriched in wild type cells in all three TMT experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the quantitative mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: No cell surface or endosomal membrane proteins were found that could represent interacting partners during the post-Golgi steps of PrP*'s trafficking itinerary to lysosomes.
source: Notably, no cell surface or endosomal membrane proteins were found that could represent interacting partners during the post-Golgi steps of PrP*'s trafficking itinerary to lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a key negative finding from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: The interaction profiles on stained gels were essentially unchanged across time points or between wild type versus ∆TMED10 cells.
source: Strikingly, the interaction profiles on the stained gels from two independent replicates were essentially unchanged across time points or between wild type versus ∆TMED10 cells (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by the stained gels in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The WT/KO ratios for nearly all GFP-PrP* interactors were very similar before versus after 60 min of ER stress.
source: Strikingly, the WT/KO ratios for nearly all GFP-PrP* interactors were very similar before (x-axis) versus after (y-axis) 60 min of ER stress (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown by the scatter plot in Figure 5E.

claim: No plausible stress-induced post-ER GFP-PrP* interactions could be detected at any time point.
source: Thus, no plausible stress-induced post-ER GFP-PrP* interactions could be detected at any time point.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis of the time-resolved mass spectrometry data.

claim: GFP-PrP* associates with both CNX and TMED10 over the entire 180 min time course after ER stress.
source: Consistent with the TMT mass spectrometry results, GFP-PrP* associated with both CNX and TMED10 over the entire 180 min time course (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 5F.

claim: The amount of CNX and TMED10 associated with GFP-PrP* was completely unchanged for 60 min after ER stress.
source: The amount that was associated was completely unchanged for 60 min.
evidence: This is shown by the immunoblotting time course in Figure 5F.

claim: GFP-PrP only transiently and weakly associates with CNX at the first time point before ER stress.
source: By contrast, GFP-PrP only transiently and weakly associated with CNX at the first time point (before ER stress), consistent with its release upon folding and egress to the cell surface.
evidence: This is shown by the immunoblotting time course in Figure 5F.

claim: GFP-PrP* retains its associations with factors of the early secretory pathway throughout its trafficking itinerary to the lysosome.
source: These results validate the mass spectrometry findings and show that GFP-PrP* retains its associations with factors of the early secretory pathway throughout its trafficking itinerary to the lysosome.
evidence: This is concluded from the time-resolved immunoblotting and mass spectrometry data.

claim: GFP-PrP* in total lysate migrates far more heterogeneously than GFP-PrP on sucrose gradients.
source: As expected from its chaperone interactions in the ER, GFP-PrP* in total lysate migrated far more heterogeneously than GFP-PrP (Figure 6A, top panels): whereas GFP-PrP was primarily in fractions 3–5, substantial amounts of GFP-PrP* were distributed across fractions 6–10 (fraction 11 represents non-solubilized material).
evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient fractionation in Figure 6A.

claim: The distribution of cell surface GFP-PrP* is more heterogeneous than cell surface GFP-PrP on sucrose gradients.
source: Similarly, the distribution of cell surface GFP-PrP* was more heterogeneous than cell surface GFP-PrP (Figure 6A, bottom panels).
evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient fractionation in Figure 6A.

claim: GFP-PrP* at the cell surface is in protein complex(es) that differ from the mostly uncomplexed GFP-PrP.
source: This difference hinted at the possibility that GFP-PrP* at the cell surface is in protein complex(es) that differ from the mostly uncomplexed GFP-PrP.
evidence: This is inferred from the different sucrose gradient distributions.

claim: GFP-PrP migrates as an uncomplexed protein without any appreciable co-purifying proteins on sucrose gradients.
source: Sucrose gradient analysis of the eluates from these surface-specific purifications showed that GFP-PrP migrates as an uncomplexed protein without any appreciable co-purifying proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient fractionation in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-PrP* co-purifies with proteins of ~75 and 90 kD that were identified as BiP and CNX.
source: By contrast, GFP-PrP* co-purified with proteins of ~75 and 90 kD that were identified by mass spectrometry and immunoblotting as BiP and CNX, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient fractionation and mass spectrometry in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Multiple independent large-scale surface purifications of cell surface GFP-PrP* contain BiP, CNX, TMED family members, and lesser amounts of other ER-resident chaperones like GRP94.
source: Multiple independent large-scale surface purifications of cell surface GFP-PrP* were analyzed by mass spectrometry and verified to contain BiP, CNX, TMED family members, and lesser amounts of other ER-resident chaperones like GRP94 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by mass spectrometry analysis of surface purifications in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Surface interactions of GFP-PrP* with chaperones are specific when compared with equal amounts of GFP-PrP purified selectively from the surface.
source: These surface interactions were validated by immunoblotting to be specific for GFP-PrP* when compared with equal amounts of GFP-PrP purified selectively from the surface (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 6C.

claim: ~ 0.1% of total CNX is recovered with surface GFP-PrP*.
source: Quantification relative to serial dilutions of total lysate indicates that ~ 0.1% of total CNX was recovered with surface GFP-PrP* (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is quantified from the immunoblotting in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CNX is recovered with surface GFP-PrP* in the proximity labeling experiment.
source: After decorating GFP-PrP* cells with Nb-APEX2, removing the excess, labeling with biotin-phenol for 1 min, and quenching, the biotinylated proteins were recovered via immobilized streptavidin. CNX was recovered as detected by immunoblotting (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown by the APEX2 proximity labeling experiment in Figure 6E.

claim: CNX is not effectively recovered in streptavidin pulldowns from GFP-PrP cells treated identically to GFP-PrP* cells.
source: When GFP-PrP cells were treated in an identical manner under conditions of equal Nb-APEX2 surface density (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), CNX was not effectively recovered in the streptavidin pulldowns (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown by the APEX2 proximity labeling experiment in Figure 6E.

claim: In live and intact cells, surface GFP-PrP* is selectively adjacent to CNX.
source: Thus, in live and intact cells, surface GFP-PrP* is selectively adjacent to CNX, which has apparently accompanied it from the ER on the way to lysosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the APEX2 proximity labeling data.

claim: FKBP*-YFP-GPI stabilized by Shield1 is primarily trafficked to the surface.
source: As expected from the study of GFP-PrP* and other GPI-anchored proteins, FKBP*-YFP-GPI stabilized by Shield1 was primarily trafficked to the surface, while FKBP*-YFP-GPI was primarily intracellular in the absence of Shield1.
evidence: This is shown by glycosylation analysis (Figure 7A), surface staining (Figure 7B), and microscopy.

claim: FKBP*-YFP-GPI is primarily intracellular in the absence of Shield1.
source: As expected from the study of GFP-PrP* and other GPI-anchored proteins, FKBP*-YFP-GPI stabilized by Shield1 was primarily trafficked to the surface, while FKBP*-YFP-GPI was primarily intracellular in the absence of Shield1.
evidence: This is shown by glycosylation analysis (Figure 7A), surface staining (Figure 7B), and microscopy.

claim: The overall level of FKBP*-YFP-GPI is lower at steady state in the absence of Shield1, consistent with its constitutive degradation.
source: The overall level of FKBP*-YFP-GPI was lower at steady state in the absence of Shield1, consistent with its constitutive degradation (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7B.

claim: Acute ER stress of FKBP*-YFP-GPI expressing cells grown in the absence of Shield1 leads to stimulation of extracellular Nb uptake.
source: Importantly, acute ER stress of FKBP*-YFP-GPI expressing cells grown in the absence of Shield1 led to a stimulation of extracellular Nb uptake (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Acute ER stress of FKBP*-YFP-GPI expressing cells grown in the absence of Shield1 leads to degradation.
source: Importantly, acute ER stress of FKBP*-YFP-GPI expressing cells grown in the absence of Shield1 led to a stimulation of extracellular Nb uptake (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Shield1-lacking FKBP*-YFP-GPI is primarily retained intracellularly and degraded via a cell surface trafficking itinerary that is stimulated by acute ER stress.
source: Thus, as with GFP-PrP*, Shield1-lacking FKBP*-YFP-GPI is primarily retained intracellularly and degraded via a cell surface trafficking itinerary that is stimulated by acute ER stress.
evidence: This is concluded from the Nb uptake and degradation data.

claim: Shield1-bound FKBP*-YFP-GPI behaves like GFP-PrP and is trafficked appropriately to the cell surface where it resides at steady state.
source: By contrast, Shield1-bound FKBP*-YFP-GPI behaves like GFP-PrP and is trafficked appropriately to the cell surface where it resides at steady state.
evidence: This is concluded from the localization and stability data.

claim: Essentially all of the initially bound Nb was still present 2 hr after Shield1 withdrawal, and these Nb molecules were still at the surface.
source: Strikingly, essentially all of the initially bound Nb was still present 2 hr after Shield1 withdrawal, and these Nb molecules were still at the surface (and hence, trypsin accessible) to the same level as that observed before withdrawal (Figure 7D, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is shown by the immunoblotting in Figure 7D.

claim: A cytosolic FKBP* tagged with blue fluorescent protein (FKBP*-BFP) was mostly degraded 2 hr after Shield1 withdrawal.
source: Importantly, a cytosolic FKBP* tagged with blue fluorescent protein (FKBP*-BFP) expressed in the same cells was fully protected from extracellular trypsin, and mostly degraded 2 hr after Shield1 withdrawal.
evidence: This is shown by the immunoblotting in Figure 7D.

claim: Acute destabilization of FKBP*-GFP-GPI at the cell surface by Shield1 withdrawal does not cause its internalization from the cell surface or degradation in lysosomes.
source: Thus, acute destabilization of FKBP*-GFP-GPI at the cell surface by Shield1 withdrawal does not cause its internalization from the cell surface or degradation in lysosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the Nb retention and lack of degradation after Shield1 withdrawal.

claim: The FKBP*-BFP in the cytosol is rapidly degraded after Shield1 withdrawal to the same low level observed when cells are grown in the absence of Shield1.
source: As expected, the FKBP*-BFP in the cytosol was rapidly degraded after Shield1 withdrawal to the same low level observed when cells are grown in the absence of Shield1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7E.

claim: The amount of FKBP*-YFP-GPI on the surface remains unchanged during the time course regardless of whether Shield1 is maintained or withdrawn.
source: In the case of FKBP*-YFP-GPI, the amount on the surface remained unchanged during the time course regardless of whether Shield1 was maintained or withdrawn.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7E.

claim: When FKBP*-YFP-GPI misfolds at the time of its biogenesis at the ER, it is degraded.
source: Taken together, these results show that when FKBP*-YFP-GPI misfolds at the time of its biogenesis at the ER, it is degraded.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing degradation when Shield1 is absent during biosynthesis.

claim: When FKBP*-YFP-GPI is allowed to go to the surface as a folded protein then misfolds, the surface population fails to be recognized as aberrant and remains there as if it were folded.
source: By contrast, when it is allowed to go to the surface as a folded protein, then misfolds, the surface population fails to be recognized as aberrant and remains there as if it were folded.
evidence: This is concluded from the Shield1 withdrawal experiments showing no degradation.

claim: Misfolding-dependent interactions made in the early secretory pathway need to be retained for cells to recognize protein misfolding at the cell surface.
source: This strongly indicates that not only is misfolding initially recognized in the ER, but the misfolding-dependent interactions made in the early secretory pathway need to be retained for cells to recognize protein misfolding at the cell surface.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential behavior of proteins misfolded in the ER vs. at the surface.

claim: FKBP*-YFP-GPI that misfolds in the ER and arrives at the surface is distinct from FKBP*-YFP-GPI that misfolds at the plasma membrane: the former is associated with intracellular factors, while the latter cannot do so.
source: Thus, FKBP*-YFP-GPI that misfolds in the ER and arrives at the surface is distinct from FKBP*-YFP-GPI that misfolds at the plasma membrane: the former is associated with intracellular factors, while the latter cannot do so.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential degradation behavior.

claim: The biochemical difference between proteins misfolded in the ER vs. at the surface appears to be a critical determinant of the misfolded protein's ultimate fate.
source: This biochemical difference between these two situations appears to be a critical determinant of the misfolded protein's ultimate fate.
evidence: This is concluded from the FKBP* experiments showing different fates.

claim: Cells transiently expose misfolded proteins to the extracellular environment.
source: The remarkable implication of this conclusion is that cells transiently expose misfolded proteins to the extracellular environment.
evidence: This is concluded from the finding that most PrP* transits the cell surface.

claim: Inhibition of endocytosis via AP2 or dynamin perturbation does not fully trap all PrP* at the cell surface and does not strongly impair degradation.
source: Indeed, inhibition of endocytosis via AP2 or dynamin perturbation, while detectably increasing the amount of PrP* at the cell surface, does not fully trap all PrP* at the cell surface and does not strongly impair degradation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the endocytosis inhibition experiments.

claim: Cells have alternative degradative options for GPI-anchored proteins including ERAD, and possibly direct Golgi-to-lysosome traffic or autophagy of the ER.
source: While this finding is difficult to interpret cleanly given the pleiotropic consequences of these manipulations for other trafficking pathways and perhaps lysosome function, it does illustrate that cells have alternative degradative options for GPI-anchored proteins including ERAD (Sikorska et al., 2016), and possibly direct Golgi-to-lysosome traffic (Coutinho et al., 2012) or autophagy of the ER (Forrester et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete block of degradation and cited literature.

claim: Surface exposure of misfolded proteins or their associated chaperones may be used to judge a cell's health or stress status by other cells in a metazoan organism.
source: One attractive idea is that perhaps surface exposure, either of misfolded proteins directly or of their associated chaperones (see below), is used to judge a cell's health or stress status by other cells in a metazoan organism (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is presented as speculation with a citation to Yu et al., 2015.

claim: Chaperones may remain tightly bound to PrP* after it leaves the ER due to the absence of co-factors that drive their recycling.
source: The chaperones may remain tightly bound after PrP* leaves the ER due to the absence of co-factors that drive their recycling, thereby preventing further attempts at folding.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative explanation for the persistent chaperone binding.

claim: The tight binding of chaperones, particularly the lectin CNX, explains why PrP*'s glycans do not get trimmed or modified during its transit through the Golgi.
source: The tight binding of chaperones, particularly the lectin CNX, nicely explains the otherwise puzzling observation that PrP*'s glycans do not get trimmed or modified during its transit through the Golgi.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of immature glycans on surface PrP* and the CNX binding data.

claim: Chaperones and cargo receptors that accompany PrP* on its degradative route are degraded in the lysosome and are essentially serving a terminal function.
source: The simplest model is that they are degraded in the lysosome and are essentially serving a terminal function.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative model for the fate of the chaperones.

claim: Elevated surface chaperones in cancer cells might reflect their involvement in degradation pathways for misfolded proteins.
source: Because cancer cells have a high mutation burden and are thought to express numerous misfolded proteins, elevated surface chaperones might reflect their involvement in degradation pathway(s) like the one described in this study.
evidence: This is presented as speculation connecting the findings to cancer biology.

claim: One role of retaining chaperone and cargo receptor interactions may be to shield the misfolded proteins from inappropriate interactions.
source: As noted above, one role of retaining chaperone and cargo receptor interactions may be to shield the misfolded proteins from inappropriate interactions.
evidence: This is presented as an inferred function of the persistent interactions.

claim: A second critical function of retaining chaperone and cargo receptor interactions is to cue endocytosis and degradation.
source: Our acute surface misfolding experiments argues that a second critical function is to cue endocytosis and degradation.
evidence: This is concluded from the FKBP* Shield1 withdrawal experiments.

claim: Cells may express a transmembrane 'receptor' for certain chaperones, and engagement of this receptor triggers endocytosis.
source: One model is that cells express a transmembrane 'receptor' for certain chaperones, and engagement of this receptor triggers endocytosis. Indeed, putative receptors that recognize chaperones have been described (Calderwood et al., 2007b), although evidence for such an interaction did not emerge from our systematic analysis of PrP* interactions.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative model with citation, but noted as not supported by the data.

claim: A GPI-anchored protein that misfolds at the cell surface goes unrecognized.
source: It is striking that a GPI-anchored protein that misfolds at the cell surface goes unrecognized.
evidence: This is concluded from the FKBP* Shield1 withdrawal experiments.

claim: In cases of quality control at the plasma membrane, the recognition factors are all in the cytosol and the clients are all integral membrane proteins with cytosolically exposed regions.
source: In these cases, the recognition factors are all in the cytosol and the clients are all integral membrane proteins with cytosolically exposed regions (Apaja et al., 2013; Apaja et al., 2010; Okiyoneda et al., 2018; Okiyoneda et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources describing plasma membrane quality control.

claim: GPI-anchored proteins as a class rely on ER-derived factors for their recognition at the plasma membrane.
source: Given that PrP* is associated with intracellular factors at the surface, we posit that GPI-anchored proteins as a class rely on this mechanism for their recognition at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is presented as a conclusion from the data on PrP* and FKBP*.
